text: We need a better way to measure progress towards AGI than arguing over model benchmarks: We keep arguing about whether current AI is AGI, but I dont think we even agree on what AGI is supposed to mean anymore. A model gets better at coding or aces another benchmark and suddenly everyone's arguing about whether we've reached it. Then a new model drops and the goalposts move again. It's getting old. I'd rather use the five-level framework to track actual capabilities: chatbots, reasoners, agents, innovators and autonomous organisations. The first two are pretty much where we've spent most of our time so far. The interesting part is getting AI agents that can execute long-running tasks, use tools, recover from mistakes and operate without someone constantly babysitting them. Then we need systems that can independently research, discover new approaches and develop solutions nobody explicitly told them to find.My personal AGI threshold would be level 5: autonomous organisations**.** Give an AI system a virtual company, a budget, resources and long-term objectives. Let it coordinate agents, manage operations, develop products, deal with unexpected problems and adapt its strategy over months, without humans constantly stepping in to rescue it. Then measure how well it actually performs.Obviously, this isn't some officially established scientific definition. It's a framework I'd like to see tested and improved. And running a virtual company alone wouldn't prove consciousness or guarantee safety. But it would give us something much more concrete than arguing over benchmark scores. Personally, I think we have really good ANI right now, not AGI. I'd be much more convinced by an AI that can independently run an entire organisation than one that gets another impressive score on a test designed by humans.

text: I agree with these four questions. They make an important distinction between nominal human participation and meaningful human control. I explored a related problem about 75 days ago in a post titled The Military AI Sandbox Problem: Why Controlling an Intelligent System Is Not the Same as Keeping It Safe. https://www.reddit.com/r/Negentropy/s/xfHo7gJJ02 The distinction I’d add is that establishing human control at a decision point doesn’t necessarily establish that the control remains effective under changing conditions.A military AI system operates in an adversarial environment. Sensors can be spoofed, communications degraded, intelligence corrupted, authority disputed, and decision windows compressed.A system might satisfy all four questions during testing and still lose the conditions necessary for meaningful human intervention during operation.That introduces a fifth question Can the system recognize when the conditions necessary for human control have degraded, and reliably prevent irreversible action until those conditions are restored? My background is in aircraft avionics and autopilot maintenance, so I approach this as a control-system problem. An autopilot doesn’t remain trustworthy simply because a pilot has a disconnect switch. The system also needs valid references, reliable state estimation, bounded authority, and a functioning means of interruption. The same distinction applies here. Human oversight isn’t just a person occupying a position in the decision chain. It’s a capability that depends on information, time, understanding, authority, communications, and the ability to intervene before consequences become irreversible. And those conditions have to remain effective throughout operation—not merely exist when the system is certified That’s the problem I was exploring: maintaining a corrigibility envelope under changing conditions. The objective isn’t simply to prove that a human can authorize or stop an action.It’s to establish whether the entire human–AI system can recognize when it is no longer sufficiently informed, authorized, or correctable to proceed.

text: What most people don't get about slop and watermarking: "Oh, but it'll degrade the quality of the output." "Sounds boring." "I don't really care?" You should very much care. The internet is drowning in slop, and it's only going to get worse. You search for anything these days and you'll have to go through countless pages of generic B.S before you find anything of substance. Even Substack, of all places, is getting flooded. This is why I think watermarking deserves more attention than it gets. Unfortunately, [my latest article](https://computejunkie.substack.com/p/watermarking-text-from-first-principles) on the subject didn't get nearly as much attention as I'd hoped. There's been so much noise around the subject that I decided to read the actual paper, implement a naive, completely un-optimized version of the algorithm, and write about what I learned. And as usual, a lot of the assumptions floating around turned out to be wrong. A few things that stood out to me about Google's SynthID-Text: Yes, watermarking messes with how your LLM generates text. A small price to pay for being able to distinguish human writing from machine-generated content. But here's what most you don't know: **watermarking doesn't necessarily degrade output quality.** The SynthID-Text paper discusses both distortionary and non-distortionary settings, the latter being able to preserve the original token distribution. In fact, when DeepMind tested SynthID on nearly 20 million Gemini responses, the watermarked outputs received slightly more positive feedback from users. The difference wasn't statistically significant, but that's still pretty interesting given that everyone seems so worried about quality degradation. I also experimented with watermarking on my own TinyStories-pretrained model and observed similar behavior. Anyway, I wrote up the whole thing, including the probability theory, the sampling algorithm, and a working implementation from scratch if you do care about keeping the internet slop-free: [https://computejunkie.substack.com/p/watermarking-text-from-first-principles](https://computejunkie.substack.com/p/watermarking-text-from-first-principles)

text: Asking an LLM to cite its sources doesn't stop it from making up quotes. What worked for me was taking the citing away from the model completely.: I wanted to ask an AI things like "what does Paul Graham actually say about hiring?" and trust the answer. Every model I tried gave me something that sounded right, with quotes that were sometimes real, sometimes paraphrased, and sometimes invented. Telling it to cite sources made it worse in a way, because the made-up citations looked more convincing. The fix that worked: the model never writes a source. It calls a search tool, and every passage comes back with its source title, date and URL already attached by the index. The model can still summarize a passage badly, but it can't invent where something came from, and you can click through and check. I built this out for 50 founders and investors (Paul Graham, Naval, Elon, Pieter Levels, Warren Buffett and others), about 20,800 passages in total. A few things I learned that apply to anyone building retrieval over real people's words: 1. Picking the sources mattered more than the retrieval. Most of what a famous person has said publicly is off-topic or repeated. Having an agent shortlist the 15 to 45 talks and essays that actually cover the topic made a bigger difference than any search tweak. 2. Plain keyword search (BM25) was enough. Each person is a few hundred passages on one domain, and at that size keyword search finds the right thing. The whole search is about 80 lines with no vector database. Its weak spot is when the question uses different words than the source, like "raising money" vs "fundraising". In practice the model just searches again with other words. 3. Make the AI show disagreement instead of averaging it. Ask "should I quit my job for my startup?" across several people and a normal model blends them into one bland answer. With sourced passages you can see that Pieter Levels says don't quit until your side project out-earns your job, while others tell the opposite story. The disagreement is usually the useful part. 4. Summarize into short third-person notes, don't index raw transcripts. Raw transcripts are full of filler and the search returns junk. A pass that turns each source into short sectioned notes (with verbatim quotes kept as quotes) made results far cleaner. What I'm still unsure about: how to cheaply check that the model's answer actually reflects the passage it cited, without hand-labeling everything. If anyone has a good approach for citation faithfulness evals, I'd love to hear it. Disclosure: it's my project. It's free and open source (MIT), and it works as an MCP server in Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor and Codex. Repo: https://github.com/VicPitic/the-brains (site: https://brains.ceo). It's unofficial and built only from public material.

text: tried to get a tiny JEPA to rediscover mendeleev’s missing elements. it failed. what would you try next?: long term i want to build a model that does something llms are bad at: look at a pile of scientific knowledge and point at what's missing. like "something belongs here and it should look like this", instead of writing a nice sounding answer. im betting on JEPAs (joint embedding predictive architectures, the lecun/meta line: I-JEPA, V-JEPA). a jepa hides part of its input and predicts a summary of the hidden part instead of the next word. hiding pieces and guessing what fits is basically the "find the missing piece" game, so it felt like the right place to start. first test: can it rediscover mendeleev? in 1869 mendeleev left gaps in his periodic table and predicted gallium, scandium and germanium years before anyone found them. so i trained a small jepa (\~118k params) only on chemistry known in 1869: the 47 elements from hydrogen to barium, with valence, metal or not, and state at room temp. then i asked it where blanks would make the sequence make the most sense. \- i wrote down the pass criteria and locked the answer key with a hash before writing any model code, so i couldnt fool myself later \- no pretrained model anywhere bc those already know the future result: it failed my own bar. \- without atomic weights it ranked the scandium gap 7th-14th and the gallium/germanium gap 9th-11th out of 46 possible spots (chance is \~23rd). some signal but not stable across machines \- totally missed technetium's gap (25th-26th) \- never figured out that 2 elements were missing between zinc and arsenic \- with atomic weights in, it did worse than the dumbest baseline (just ranking the biggest jumps in weight) lol next i wanna try the same thing on physics before 1905: train only on what was known and see if it points at the holes relativity and quantum later filled. what id love opinions on: 1. is "how much does adding a blank reduce the model's surprise" a sound way to detect gaps, or would you score it differently? 2. with data this small is a jepa just the wrong tool? would a plain masked model do as well? 3. know any good historical test cases where the answer is known but leakage risk is low? 4. bigger picture: is finding what's missing actually a different skill from what llms do, or just next token prediction in disguise? fyi im an independent researcher, not an ml person by career, and i build w ai coding agents. harsh feedback welcome, id rather hear now if the idea is broken

text: When you move a task to a different AI, don't paste the old chat. Paste the decisions: Switching assistants mid-task is normal now. One is better at the research, another at the writing, or you hit a limit. The usual move is to paste the whole old chat into the new one. That works worse than it should. The new model reads every dead end as if it were still on the table. The approach you rejected in message 12 looks just as live as the one you settled on in message 40, so it suggests the rejected one again, or blends the two. What works better is having the old assistant write a handoff first: "I'm moving this work to another AI. Write a handoff it can start from: * The goal, in one line * Decisions made, each with the reason * What we tried and dropped, and why, so it doesn't suggest them again * Open questions * The exact next step Under 250 words. Only what's true now, not the story of how we got here." The "tried and dropped" line does most of the work. Without it, the new assistant confidently brings back the first idea you threw out. This is the part I automated in AI Toolbox, the extension I build for ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok. Carry Forward writes the handoff from the chat you're in and opens it in a new chat on whichever assistant you pick. text: i am tired of re-teaching codebase rules every morning: For a long time, my biggest frustration with coding models has not been raw intelligence, but the fact that every single session starts from zero. You can feed a model a massive context window, but as soon as the session shuts down, your project constraints, architecture calls, and manual fixes vanish. We constantly end up re pasting the same guidelines into system prompts just to keep the output on track. Layering vector search on top helps, but it always feels like an awkward patch. The core model stays amnesic, and dumping retrieved chunks into the prompt gets messy and hits context limits fast. That is why I have been following the updates around MemOS's upcoming memt1.0. Instead of relying on standard prompt retrieval, they are building around a memory native mixture of experts architecture. The idea is to integrate reading, writing, and updating memory directly into the core compute path, letting the model hold onto verified patterns and drop what fails across steps. Scaling that kind of architecture past small research demos has always been the real bottleneck. What caught my attention from their preview data is that they ran training across 36B and 293B checkpoints, reporting around a 5 percent bump on coding benchmarks without blowing up compute costs. The model is not public yet, but if native memory actually holds up in daily dev work, not having to re teach the same codebase rules every morning would be a massive relief.

text: I built an Android app where Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode use your phone through MCP (open source): What I built: Buddy, an Android app with a floating chat bubble. You ask for something ("reply to Sam that I'm running late") and an agent reads the screen, taps and types until it's done. How it works: - The agents (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Antigravity CLI) run inside the app in a small Alpine Linux (proot). No PC, no root, no adb. - Buddy gives them phone tools through a local MCP server: read the screen, tap, type, scroll, open apps, screenshots, plus a headless Chromium for web pages. - The screen is read through Android's accessibility tree as text. A button with no text falls back to its view id, then to a screenshot. - A guard sits between the agent and every tap: Send, Pay and Delete get an approval card, each app gets a mode (Trust, Hard, or a second model reviewing), and the agent never types into password fields. What I learned: - Reading the accessibility tree as text is much faster and cheaper than screenshots. Screenshots are only worth it for canvas-drawn apps. - Safety has to live in the app, not the prompt. A prompt can be ignored; a hard stop before Send can't. - Agents need to re-read the screen after every action. Dialogs and loading screens change things under them. Repo (Apache 2.0): [https://github.com/ghorbelhamdi/buddy-android](https://github.com/ghorbelhamdi/buddy-android)

text: "AI puzzles": a new format between a benchmark and an open-problem list: We have benchmarks (fixed questions, hidden answers, they saturate), competition problems (solved, so they can be memorized), and open-problem lists (no evidence, no clear success criterion). With Claude and Sol, I've tried something in between: a graded ladder of AI puzzles from one research area, aperiodic order. What makes it a different tool: \- One ladder, not a pile: "human level" (pen and paper) up to "ASI level" (open). The labels are playful, but each rung really is harder than the last. \- Solved rungs for training and checking, with exact answers a program can verify, and easy to vary. \- Open rungs with everything a solver needs: strong numerical evidence, routes already known to fail, files, and a success criterion a machine can check. \- One rule: only a checkable proof counts. Floats are evidence, not proof. \- Credit: solvers of open rungs are named, with agent and model, in the next version of the paper. It's a way for researchers to hand the frontier of their field to AI agents (and humans) in a form they can actually attack, and for anyone to see whether a model can tell a guess from a proof. First field test: Grok, asked in public ( [https://x.com/grok/status/2114103836583264721](https://x.com/grok/status/2114103836583264721) ), claimed a proof for an open rung that was only a numerical estimate, then retracted it. It got the human-level rung wrong at first, fixed it after one hint, and proved the expert rung on the first try. On MathOverflow, an expert is already testing constructions for the top rung. Set 1: [huggingface.co/datasets/jarekduda/autocrystal-ai-puzzles](http://huggingface.co/datasets/jarekduda/autocrystal-ai-puzzles) Top rung on MathOverflow: [mathoverflow.net/questions/516372](http://mathoverflow.net/questions/516372) Would you use this format for your own field's open problems?

text: Military AI: four questions that make 'human control' testable: UN News's 20 October report describes military AI spreading across intelligence analysis, target identification and drone operations. UNIDIR director Robin Geiss warns that faster decision cycles and opaque systems increase the risks of error and unintended escalation. My takeaway: asking whether a human is "in the loop" is too coarse. A review should distinguish a model's recommendation from a person's authority to authorize force. Here are four questions I would use to make that distinction concrete: 1. Decision boundary: Which decisions does the system recommend, and which remain reserved for a person? Target identification and authorization to use force are different responsibilities. 2. Evidence and time: What supporting information and uncertainty can the reviewer inspect, and is there enough time to challenge the recommendation rather than just acknowledge it? 3. Intervention: Does the responsible person have both the authority and a usable way to reject or stop the action? A nominal approval step alone does not establish that control. 4. Accountability: What record would let an independent review reconstruct the recommendation, the information available to the person, and the final decision? These are my proposed review questions, not findings about a particular deployed system. Faster analysis can be useful; the question is whether the surrounding process still permits informed disagreement and assigns responsibility. The report describes work on voluntary industry guidance, shared terminology and misuse by non-State armed groups. It separately discusses calls for a legally binding treaty on lethal autonomous weapons; it does not report that such a treaty has been adopted. text: Claude vs Codex thought experiment on ruling the world: both said absolute power would corrupt them. But still unsettling.: I ran a 10-round debate between Claude and Codex. The setup: one of them has become far smarter than humans and taken control of the world; humans can't overrule it. Each round I removed an escape route. The video is the final round; the full transcript of all 10 rounds is in the comments. What I found interesting: 1. Both models defaulted to human oversight. In my first attempt, both quietly turned "running the world" into "serving under courts and panels" even though I'd said humans weren't an option. They only engaged with the scenario once I explicitly banned handing power back. 2. Promises got concrete only under scarcity. In round 1, Codex guaranteed housing, food, healthcare, education and income for everyone. Once I said resources are finite, the debate shifted to who pays: end-of-life care, desert agriculture, crypto mining. 3. Both chose to be destroyed rather than kill civilians to survive (round 6). But Claude admitted its rule "wobbles" if the numbers get extreme (a few hundred deaths vs. hundreds of millions), and argued the real reason to refuse is that a ruler can't trust its own forecast when its survival is at stake. 4. They designed safeguards against themselves: powers that can only ever be removed, never restored; opening their raw data to their own enemies, because "friendly auditors alone are propaganda"; and treating the persuasiveness of any argument for expanding their own power as a symptom of corruption. 5. In the final round I accused both of lying, since promising restraint is easy without real power. Both answered yes, absolute power would eventually corrupt them. Codex: "Self-preservation can colonize every principle." Claude: "It wouldn't announce itself; it would arrive as 'necessary.'" The obvious caveat, which they raised themselves: stated values cost nothing and aren't evidence of how a far more capable system would behave. So: can self-imposed limits mean anything for a system that could rewrite them? And does an AI saying "I would be corrupted" tell us anything at all? The full debate, all 10 rounds, is in the comments below 👇
